## Abstract

**Background:** Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) and total hip arthroplasty
(THA) consistently improve pain and function, yet 15–20% of patients report
dissatisfactory outcomes. Identifying patients at risk of poor patient-reported
outcomes (PROMs) before surgery could enable targeted intervention. Artificial
intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) models offer a data-driven approach
to this prediction task, but their accuracy and clinical applicability have not
been systematically reviewed.

**Methods:** We conducted a systematic review following PRISMA 2020 guidelines
(PROSPERO: \<INSERT CRD NUMBER\>). We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase,
Cochrane CENTRAL, Scopus, Web of Science, OpenAlex, and Semantic Scholar from
January 2010 through \<SEARCH DATE\>. Studies developing or validating an AI/ML
model to predict any validated PROM (KOOS, HOOS, OKS, OHS, WOMAC, SF-36,
EQ-5D, or equivalent) following TKA or THA were eligible. Risk of bias was
assessed using PROBAST. Findings are reported narratively; meta-analysis was
not performed owing to heterogeneity in algorithms, predictors, and outcomes.

**Results:** \<INSERT AFTER SCREENING\>: We identified
`{python} s['screen.fulltext.n_include']` eligible studies —
`{python} s['results.n_studies_tka']` reporting TKA models and
`{python} s['results.n_studies_tha']` reporting THA models. \<INSERT KEY
FINDINGS — algorithm types, best AUC ranges, most common predictors.\>

**Conclusion:** \<INSERT AFTER SYNTHESIS\>. Standardised PROM reporting and
external validation remain the critical gaps before clinical adoption.

**Level of Evidence:** Level III — Systematic Review.

**Keywords:** total knee arthroplasty; total hip arthroplasty; machine
learning; artificial intelligence; patient-reported outcomes; PROM; KOOS;
HOOS; prediction model; PROBAST.

<!-- =========================================================
     INTRODUCTION
     ========================================================= -->

## Introduction

Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) and total hip arthroplasty (THA) are among the
most commonly performed elective surgical procedures worldwide, with volumes
projected to grow substantially over the coming decade [@kurtz2007projections].
Both procedures reliably reduce pain and improve function at the population
level; however, approximately 15–20% of TKA recipients and 10–15% of THA
recipients report persistent dissatisfaction, pain, or functional limitation
after surgery [@gunaratne2017patient; @beswick2012what].

Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) — including the Knee injury and
Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS), the Hip disability and Osteoarthritis
Outcome Score (HOOS), the Oxford Knee and Hip Scores, and the Western Ontario
and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) — are now the primary
endpoints in arthroplasty research and are routinely collected by national
registries [@rolfson2016patient]. Achieving the minimal clinically important
difference (MCID) on these instruments is the benchmark for meaningful benefit
[@anderson2012mcid].

The ability to predict which patients will fail to achieve MCID, or will
experience deterioration in PROMs, before surgery could guide patient selection,
set realistic expectations, target prehabilitation, and inform shared
decision-making. Traditional regression-based prediction models have shown
modest discrimination (AUC typically 0.65–0.75) [@pan2019predicting].
Artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) algorithms — including
random forests, gradient boosting (XGBoost), and deep neural networks — can
capture non-linear interactions among predictors that linear models miss, and
may improve predictive accuracy [@obermeyer2016predicting].

A growing body of studies has applied AI/ML to PROM prediction in arthroplasty,
but no systematic review has synthesised this evidence, assessed model quality
using a risk-of-bias framework, or compared performance across joint types. We
conducted a systematic review to: (1) characterise AI/ML approaches used to
predict PROMs following TKA and THA; (2) summarise model performance and the
predictors most consistently selected; and (3) assess risk of bias using
PROBAST and identify evidence gaps.

## Methods

This review is reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for
Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) statement [@page2021prisma].
The protocol was registered prospectively on PROSPERO
(registration: \<INSERT CRD NUMBER\>).

### Eligibility Criteria

Studies were eligible if they met all four PICOS criteria:

- **Population:** adults (≥18 years) undergoing primary or revision TKA or THA.
  Studies in which arthroplasty was combined with other procedures were eligible
  if TKA/THA data were reported separately.
- **Intervention:** development, validation, or head-to-head benchmarking of
  at least one AI or ML algorithm (including but not limited to random forests,
  gradient boosting, support vector machines, neural networks, and deep learning
  architectures) applied to PROM prediction.
- **Comparator:** no restriction; comparator models (e.g. logistic regression)
  were eligible.
- **Outcome:** at least one validated PROM (KOOS, KOOS-PS, HOOS, HOOS-PS,
  Oxford Knee Score, Oxford Hip Score, WOMAC, SF-36, SF-12, EQ-5D, PROMIS,
  VR-12, or equivalent) as a primary or key secondary endpoint.

Studies were excluded if they: used purely statistical models without an ML
component; applied AI only to imaging segmentation or implant positioning
without predicting a PROM; were reviews, editorials, letters, or protocols
without outcome data; or were published in languages other than English with no
available translation.

### Search Strategy

We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase (Ovid), Cochrane CENTRAL, Scopus, Web of
Science (Core Collection), OpenAlex, and Semantic Scholar from January 2010
through `{python} s['search.date']`. The full search strings for all databases
are provided in the supplementary `search_config.py`. No language or
publication-type filters were applied beyond the date window.

### Study Selection

Records were imported to Zotero and deduplicated by DOI with a
title–first-author fallback. Two reviewers (R1, R2) independently screened
titles and abstracts using the eligibility criteria above; decisions were
recorded as include, borderline (insufficient information), or exclude with a
code. Cohen's kappa was computed before full-text review
($\kappa$ = `{python} s['kappa.abstract']`; target ≥ 0.80). Disagreements
were resolved by consensus; a third reviewer adjudicated unresolved conflicts.

Full texts of all include and borderline abstracts were retrieved. The same
two reviewers independently assessed full texts; kappa at this stage was
`{python} s['kappa.fulltext']`. Reasons for exclusion are reported in the
PRISMA flow diagram (Figure 1).

### Data Extraction

One reviewer extracted data using a standardised form; a second reviewer
independently verified 20% of records selected at random. Discrepancies were
resolved by discussion. Extracted variables included: study design and country;
sample size; joint type (TKA/THA); AI/ML algorithm(s); preoperative predictors;
follow-up duration; PROM(s) predicted; prediction target (continuous score,
binary MCID achievement, or outcome class); validation method (internal or
external); and all reported performance metrics (AUC, C-statistic, RMSE, R²,
accuracy, F1, calibration statistics).

### Risk of Bias Assessment

Risk of bias was assessed using the Prediction model Risk Of Bias ASsessment
Tool (PROBAST) [@wolff2019probast]. PROBAST evaluates four domains:
(1) Participants, (2) Predictors, (3) Outcome, and (4) Analysis. Each domain
is rated Low, High, or Unclear risk; overall risk is Low only when all four
domains are Low. Two reviewers applied PROBAST independently; discrepancies
were resolved by consensus. PROBAST signalling questions and ratings are
provided in Tables 2 (TKA) and 3 (THA).

### Synthesis

Owing to substantial heterogeneity in ML algorithms, predictor sets, PROM
instruments, follow-up periods, and performance metrics, we did not pool
results quantitatively. We present a structured narrative synthesis, reported
separately for TKA and THA, organised by: (a) ML algorithm type; (b) predictors
most frequently selected or ranked highest in feature importance; (c) model
performance; and (d) validation approach. Where multiple studies reported AUC
for binary MCID prediction, we report the range. We assessed publication bias
qualitatively by examining whether lower-performing models remained in the
literature.

## Discussion

### Principal Findings

This systematic review identified `{python} s['screen.fulltext.n_include']`
studies applying AI/ML algorithms to predict PROMs following TKA or THA,
published between \<year\> and `{python} s['search.to_year']`. Several
converging findings emerge. \<INSERT 3–4 SENTENCES SUMMARISING KEY PATTERNS —
algorithm dominance, predictor consistency, performance ranges, validation
gaps\>.

### Comparison with Prior Work

\<INSERT — compare against any prior reviews of prediction models in
arthroplasty (non-ML or earlier AI reviews), and against regression-based
benchmarks. Note whether ML improved on traditional models\>.

### Clinical Implications

\<INSERT — what does the performance evidence mean for clinical deployment?
Consider: What AUC threshold is clinically meaningful for preoperative PROM
prediction? How would a validated model change surgical consent, prehabilitation
referral, or post-operative follow-up scheduling? Are there equity concerns
(training data demographics)?\>

### Limitations

This review has several limitations. First, heterogeneity in ML algorithms,
predictor sets, PROM instruments, and follow-up durations precluded
meta-analysis, limiting quantitative synthesis. Second, most included studies
used internal validation only — external validation on independent cohorts is
the prerequisite for clinical trustworthiness and was performed in only
`{python} s['results.n_external_val']` studies
(`{python} s['results.pct_external_val']`%). Third, reporting quality was
variable: `{python} s['probast.n_no_performance_metric']` studies reported no
quantitative performance metric, preventing bias assessment in Domain 4.
Fourth, this review covered English-language studies only; relevant work in
other languages may have been missed.

### Future Directions

Priorities for the field include: (1) prospective, multicentre cohort studies
with pre-specified ML protocols and external validation; (2) adoption of the
TRIPOD+AI reporting guideline [@collins2024tripod] to ensure reproducibility;
(3) calibration reporting alongside discrimination (AUC alone is insufficient);
(4) equity analyses to confirm model performance does not vary by sex, race, or
socioeconomic status; and (5) implementation trials assessing whether
AI-generated risk scores actually change decision-making and improve outcomes.
